meta.title: Who really said "The aim of art is to represent not the outward appearance of things, but their inward significance"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Widely credited to Aristotle, but the wording is Will Durant's 1926 paraphrase in The Story of Philosophy — his summary of Aristotle, not Aristotle's own words.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The aim of art is to represent not the outward appearance of things, but their inward significance'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Aristotle. The phrasing is Will Durant's, from The Story of Philosophy (1926) — his paraphrase of Aristotle's theory of art, not a genuine quotation.

answer.label: Not Aristotle — actually Will Durant
answer.authorDates: 1885–1981 · American historian & philosopher; wrote it in 1926
answer.sourceLine: The sentence is Will Durant’s own prose from The Story of Philosophy (1926), where he summarizes Aristotle’s theory of art. Durant introduces the idea with “says Aristotle,” but the words are his — the line appears nowhere in Aristotle’s surviving works.

source.heading: Where it really comes from

docMeta.dd: Ch. II, “Psychology and the Nature of Art”

source.excerpt: Yet the aim of art is to represent not the outward appearance of things, but their inward significance; for this, and not the external mannerism and detail, is their reality.
trail: The quote is mass-credited to Aristotle on Goodreads and similar aggregators, always with no work cited.
A fuller reproduction of Durant’s Aristotle chapter shows the sentence in context, prefaced “says Aristotle,” as Durant’s own summary prose.
Reference pages that cite anything trace it to Durant’s The Story of Philosophy, Ch. II, part VI — not to Aristotle.
The book itself is on the Internet Archive, with the “Psychology and the Nature of Art” section in the Aristotle chapter.
source.cutTag: ↑ the popular quote lops off Durant's closing clause
source.excerptNote: In the book the sentence is introduced by “says Aristotle” and sits inside Durant’s own running paraphrase (“Essentially the form of art is an imitation of reality; it holds the mirror up to nature…”). It is Durant’s compression of Aristotle’s ideas about mimesis, not a translated quotation.

author.name: Will Durant
author.heading: About Will Durant
author.bio: Will Durant was an American writer and historian best known for The Story of Philosophy (1926), a hugely popular survey that made academic philosophy accessible to a mass audience. With his wife Ariel he later wrote the eleven-volume The Story of Civilization, winning a Pulitzer Prize in 1968. His gift for vivid summary is exactly why so many of his paraphrases — this line, and the famous “we are what we repeatedly do… excellence is a habit” — now circulate as if Aristotle himself had written them.

misattribution.heading: The misattribution
misattribution.intro: The line is one of the most widely shared “Aristotle” quotes on the internet, yet none of the sites that post it can name a work — because there isn’t one. The words are Will Durant’s.

items.why: Quote aggregators credit Aristotle with no cited work; the wording matches no passage in his surviving texts and instead reproduces Durant’s 1926 paraphrase, which merely opens with “says Aristotle.”

misattribution.truthLine: The idea — that art imitates reality to reveal its inner significance — is genuinely Aristotelian, drawn from the Poetics; the memorable sentence is Will Durant’s, from The Story of Philosophy (1926).

context.heading: Why it gets misread
lead: Durant’s The Story of Philosophy works by paraphrase: he condenses each thinker into brisk, quotable prose, often folding his own summarizing sentences right after phrases like “says Aristotle.” Read at speed — or clipped for a quote card — those summaries look exactly like direct quotations.

That is how this line, and several other ‘Aristotle’ favorites from the same book, escaped into the world under Aristotle’s name. The underlying thought is faithful to Aristotle’s account of mimesis in the Poetics; the polished wording is Durant’s twentieth-century voice.
context.pull: Faithful to Aristotle’s idea — but written by his 1926 popularizer, Will Durant.
